L66: Measurement and correction of atmospheric effects in O 2-B and O 2-A absorption
L67: bands in the context of sun-induced fluorescence remote sensing
L68: 
L69: F. Daumard a, Y. Goulas a, A. Ounis a, R. Pedros b, I. Moya a
L70: 
L71: a Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique, Ecole Polytechnique, 91128 Palaiseau, France
L72: 
L73: b Universitat de Valencia, Departament de Fisica de la Terra i Termodinamica, Valencia, Spain,
L74: 
L75: ABSTRACT
L76: 
L77: Under sun light illumination, the shape of the atmospheric oxygen
L78: 
L79: bands (O 2-B, 687 nm and O 2-A, 760 nm) of the vegetation
L80: radiance is modified by chlorophyll fluorescence. However for far-
L81: 
L82: range measurements, atmospheric effects also modify this shape.
L83: 
L84: In this study, measurements in O 2-A and O 2-B absorption bands
L85: 
L86: have been performed at different altitudes up to 3123 m over bare
L87: 
L88: soil and wheat fields. It is observed that bands depth increase
L89: 
L90: significantly with altitude. In O 2-B band, the total magnitude of
L91: 
L92: variation is of the same order of magnitude as the change induced
L93: by vegetation fluorescence, while it is much greater in O 2-A band.
L94: 
L95: We used MODTRAN 4 to correct measurements from these
L96: 
L97: atmospheric effect and to retrieve ground level band depths. It is
L98: 
L99: found that the variation of corrected band depth with altitude is
L100: 
L101: greatly reduced. These results show that MODTRAN 4 can be
L102: 
L103: used to account for atmospheric effects. We also showed that an
L104: 
L105: accurate evaluation of the contribution of environment is needed to
L106: correct band depth from atmospheric effects, especially in the O 2-B
L107: 
L108: band.
L109: 
L110: Index Terms - Atmospheric correction, sun-induced
L111: 
L112: fluorescence, oxygen absorption band, passive measurements
L113: 
L114: 1. INTRODUCTION
L115: 
L116: At global scale, photosynthesis is the largest process of
L117: 
L118: atmospheric carbon fixation by the terrestrial surface. The
L119: 
L120: estimation of the amount of carbon exchanged between
L121: 
L122: atmosphere and vegetation is crucial for predicting the evolution of
L123: 
L124: atmospheric CO 2. However, the uncertainty on global
L125: photosynthesis activity has a strong impact on this estimate. The
L126: 
L127: current observations of land surfaces allow to characterize the state
L128: 
L129: of the vegetation (cover, light interception, biomass) but rather
L130: 
L131: poorly its functioning. The measurement of chlorophyll
L132: 
L133: fluorescence (ChlF) is seen as a way to assess the photosynthetic
L134: 
L135: activity of plants. Indeed, chlorophyll fluorescence is emitted after
L136: 
L137: the absorption of light by pigments and therefore is in competition
L138: with the use of light for photosynthesis. Thus, the variations of
L139: 
L140: fluorescence yield provide information on photosynthetic yield
L141: 
L142: changes.
L143: 
L144: Chlorophyll fluorescence is widely used in the laboratory at
L145: 
L146: the leaf level [1]. But the current challenge is to achieve such
L147: 
L148: measurement at larger scale on a routine basis. At leaf level, the
L149: 
L150: fluorescence is commonly measured using artificial excitation
L151: 
L152: sources. As active methods have a rather limited range, the method
L153: commonly adopted up to now to measure at larger distance is a
L154: 
L155: passive method that allow the measurement of solar-induced
L156: 
L157: fl uorescence. Passive methods use the abrupt changes in solar
L158: 
L159: illumination for discriminating chlorophyll fluorescence from the
L160: 
L161: irradiance reflected by the vegetation. The majority of the studies
L162: 
L163: focus on the use of atmospheric oxygen absorption band at 687 nm
L164: 
L165: (O 2-B) and 760 nm (O 2-A) induced by the oxygen present in the
L166: atmosphere. These bands have the advantage of being relatively
L167: 
L168: broad and are particularly well spectrally-located with respect to
L169: 
L170: the chlorophyll fluorescence spectrum: they are close to both
L171: 
L172: fluorescence peak at 685 and 740 nm.
L173: 
L174: The first airborne measurements of chlorophyll fluorescence
L175: 
L176: in both oxygen bands were achieved in 2005 [2] and now sun-
L177: 
L178: induced fluorescence measurements from space is considered [3,
L179: 
L180: 4]. At such distance, the effects induced by the atmosphere must be
L181: 
L182: taken into account.
L183: Many methods have been proposed to retrieve fluorescence
L184: 
L185: from passive measurement in the oxygen absorption bands. A ll
L186: 
L187: these methods use the abrupt changes of irradiance caused by the
L188: 
L189: oxygen absorption for discriminating the fluorescence from
L190: 
L191: reflected irradiance. In this study, rather than studying the full
L192: 
L193: radiance spectrum of oxygen absorption bands, we chose to focus
L194: 
L195: on radiance at two wavelengths, one is chosen outside the
L196: 
L197: absorption band (off-band) where there is no absorption, and the
L198: other one is chosen inside the band (in-band) where absorption is
L199: 
L200: maximum. Hence, with a simplified instrumentation (AirFLEX
L201: 
L202: sensor, see [2]), we are able to capture the essential absorption and
L203: 
L204: scattering processes that occur within and outside the oxygen
L205: 
L206: bands. The two radiances allow to compute t he depth of the
L207: 
L208: oxygen absorption bands which is defined as the ratio between the
L209: 
L210: off-band flux and the in-band flux. The depth is a measurement of
L211: the spectral variation of irradiance. Moreover, in an ideal case, the
L212: 
L213: measurement of the depth variation induced by the vegetation is
L214: 
L215: sufficient to obtain an estimate of fluorescence.
L216: 
L217: The objective of this paper is to study the variation of oxygen
L218: 
L219: absorption band depth with the altitude and to correc t
L220: 
L221: measurements from atmospheric effects. This study is based on
L222: 
L223: measurements made during the airborne campaign SEN2FLEX
L224: 
L225: (SENtinel-2 and FLuorescence EXperiment) which was carried
L226: 
L227: out in summer 2005.
L228: 2. MATERIAL AND METHODS
L229: 
L230: The chosen experimental area was located in Barrax within La
L231: 
L232: Mancha, a plateau 700 m above sea level in the south of Spain.
L233: 
L234: The area around Barrax has been used for agricultural research for
L235: 
L236: many years. It is characterized by a flat morphology and large
L237: 
L238: agricultural fields.
L239: 
L240: Measurements were made using the AirFLEX sensor
L241: 
L242: developed in the framework of the Earth Observation Preparatory
L243: 
L244: Program of the European Space Agency. It is a six channel sensor
L245: that provides simultaneous radiance measurement in both O 2-A
L246: 
L247: and O 2-B bands. For each absorption band, three measurements are
L248: 
L249: performed: one in-band and two off-band, on the continuum.
L250: 
L251: AirFLEX was installed in a downward viewing configuration on a
L252: 
L253: Cessna C 208B Gran Caravan aircraft provided by the German
L254: 
L255: Space Agency (DLR). The footprint at an altitude of 350 m was
L256: 
L257: about 12 m. The measurements were repeated at four altitudes: 324
L258: 
L259: m, 645 m, 1254 m and 3123 m above ground. In order to minimize
L260: variations of the sunlight optical path during measurements, flights
L261: 
L262: were done around solar noon.
L263: 
L264: Atmosphere characterization: during the measurement campaign,
L265: 
L266: two meteorological balloons equipped with a Vaisala RS80
L267: 
L268: radiosonde were released each day to characterize pressure,
L269: 
L270: temperature and humidity profiles. One in the early morning before
L271: 
L272: the mixing layer develops, the second around 11:00 UTC, to
L273: 
L274: characterize the precise water vapor profile in the lower layers
L275: which change rapidly because of solar heating.
L276: 
L277: Aerosol properties have been monitored by the Solar
L278: 
L279: Radiation Team of the University of Valencia. The retrieved
L280: 
L281: aerosol properties include: absorption spectrum, extinction
L282: 
L283: spectrum, asymmetry factor as well as phase function in the
L284: 
L285: 40 0 nm – 800 nm range with 50 nm steps.
L286: 
L287: In this study we used MODTRAN version 4 v1r1 (MODerate
L288: 
L289: Spectral Resolution Atmospheric TRANsmittance Algorithm) [5-
L290: 
L291: 7]. MODTRAN, is a radiative transfer code developed by Spectral
L292: Sciences, Inc and the Air Force Laboratory/Space Vehicles
L293: 
L294: Directorate (AFRL/VS). The resolution in our wavelength range is
L295: 
L296: 1 cm-1.
L297: 
L298: 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
L299: 
L300: 3.1. Experimental results
L301: 
L302: Concerning the remote sensing of chlorophyll fluorescence, two
L303: 
L304: types of target are particularly interesting: vegetation and non-
L305: 
L306: fluorescent target, bare soil for example [2]. W e choo se to focus on
L307: 
L308: a small portion of a flight containing these two types of targets.
L309: Thus, in the following, we will study a small part of one flight
L310: 
L311: constituted by data from a wheat field (ρ 687 ~ 0.035, ρ 760 ~ 0.41,
L312: 
L313: NDVI ~ 0.84) and a bare soil (ρ 687 ~ 0.26, ρ 760 ~ 0.29, NDVI ~
L314: 
L315: 0.05).
L316: 
L317: Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 shows the evolution of O 2-B and O 2-A
L318: 
L319: absorption band depth with altitude averaged over each field. The
L320: 
L321: modification of the shape of the absorption band induced by
L322: 
L323: vegetation is clearly visible. For example at 324 m in O 2-B band
L324: (Fig. 1), the depth goes from 1.45 on bare soil to 1.38 on wheat
L325: 
L326: field. In the same time, the O 2-A band depth goes from 4.3 on the
L327: 
L328: bare soil to 4.09 on wheat field (Fig. 2). On both bands, the band
L329: 
L330: depth increase with altitude. In O 2-B band, the total increase is
L331: 
L332: about 10 % on wheat field and about 7 % on bare field, 30 % and
L333: 
L334: 35 % respectively in O 2-A band. The contribution of the vegetation
L335: 
L336: to the modification of the absorption band depth is the difference
L337: between the vegetation’s curve and the bare soil’s curve. Hence, it
L338: 
L339: can be seen that the O 2-B band depth variation induced by altitude
L340: 
L341: (from 3 24 m to 31 23 m), i.e. by atmospheric effects, is in the same
L342: 
L343: order of magnitude than the vegetation contribution. In O 2-A band,
L344: 
L345: the atmospheric effects are even greater than the vegetation
L346: 
L347: contribution.
L348:

L350: 
L351: corrected (measurements on bare soil and on a wheat field)
L352: Fig. 2: O 2-A band depth variation with altitude measured and
L353: 
L354: corrected (measurements on bare soil and on a wheat field)
